A fork is moulded, dropped in a bin, cut off its runner, and marked by a laser. Always in that order.
Somebody wrote that order down once, so every fork follows it. That written-down road is a routing.
Here are the three machines of that road, on the floor right now.
Three words. An operation is one step, done on one machine: moulding, on the mould.
A sequence is the step's number. Ten comes before twenty, twenty before thirty. The gaps leave room to add a step later.
And a routing is the operations in sequence, for one material. The fork's routing is moulding, then degating, then marking.
A routing is a recipe, but a recipe of steps, not of ingredients.
What goes in, the resin and the plate, is the bill of materials. The routing says what is done to it, in what order, and where.
Every order for a material runs that material's routing. So the routing is where the floor's work starts.
This is where a plant keeps its routings: Admin, Routings. Sixty-one of them on this plant, one for each line.
The first row is the fork line's. Step ten, Mold, on FORK1_Mold. Then twenty, Degate. Then thirty, Mark.
Beside every step is the cost center it bills to, CC-MOULD01. Nobody typed that into the routing: it comes from the machine's line.
The plant already has a pallet routing for each palletizing line. Here they are: RT-PAL1 to RT-PAL4.
Now we define one of our own from scratch, in the form below: RT-PALLET, a second way to make the pallet on line PAL1.
A code, a name, and the material it makes: PALLET, the outbound pallet of wrapped sets.
Step ten, Palletizer, on the machine PAL1_Palletizer. Watch the end of the machine's line in the form.
Cost center CC-PAL01. We did not type it. The form read it from the line the machine is on.
Add an operation. It numbers itself twenty. StretchWrap, on PAL1_StretchWrap, the same line, so the same cost center.
Create the routing.
There it is in the table: RT-PALLET, for PALLET, ten Palletizer then twenty StretchWrap, each with its cost center.
From now on an order for a pallet can be made this way, and every step knows where it happens and what it bills to.
Now the things it refuses. First, a routing with no steps at all: a code, a name, and no operation.
Refused: a routing needs at least one operation. A material with no steps cannot be made.
Second, the same code twice. We type RT-PALLET again, with one step.
Refused: that code already exists. A routing's code names one routing, so an order can say which road it takes.
A step on a machine that does not exist cannot even be asked. The list holds only this plant's own tree, from the company down to each machine.
And the material is a list with no blank, so it always says something: here, still PALLET. Check it says what you mean before you press create.
That is a routing: the road a material takes, step by step, machine by machine. You now know how to do three things.
